title: Data-driven decision making: a framework that goes beyond dashboards
summary: Data-driven decision making ties specific decisions to evidence. Here's a practical framework for doing it well, beyond just building more dashboards.
body_text: Data-driven decision making is the practice of tying a specific decision to specific evidence before you make it, then checking later whether the evidence was right. It is not the same as having dashboards, tracking KPIs, or being “data-informed.” A team can have hundreds of charts and still make every real choice on instinct, politics, or whoever spoke last in the meeting. This is a framework for teams that already have the data but still struggle to act on it. It covers what actually separates a data-driven decision from a decorated one, an original loop for running decisions, a rubric for whether a metric is good enough to bet on, a lightweight decision brief, the failure modes that quietly creep back in, and an honest section on when you should not wait for data at all. TL;DR A decision is data-driven only if you can name the decision, the owner, the evidence, and the threshold that would change your mind before you act. Dashboards are inputs, not decisions. Most teams over-invest in building charts and under-invest in connecting those charts to specific, owned choices. The useful unit of work is the decision loop: frame the question, set the threshold, gather evidence, decide, record, and review. The review step is the one almost everyone skips. A metric is “decision-grade” when it is defined once, owned, fresh enough for the decision, and directly tied to the action under consideration. Most vanity metrics fail at least two of those tests. The maturity ladder goes from reactive to instrumented to decision-grade to learning. Moving up is a process and culture change, not a tooling purchase. Sometimes the right call is to decide without data: when the cost of waiting exceeds the cost of being wrong, or when the decision is cheap and reversible. Why having dashboards is not the same as deciding with data Most companies that call themselves data-driven have solved the easy half of the problem. They have a warehouse, a BI tool, and dashboards for revenue, activation, churn, and pipeline. The numbers are visible. What is missing is the link between those numbers and the choices people actually make. The gap shows up in predictable ways. A team debates a pricing change for three weeks, pulls five different charts, and then ships the version the loudest executive preferred anyway. A growth team launches a feature, watches a dashboard tick up, and declares victory without ever stating what number would have meant failure. A board deck shows twelve metrics, none of which changes what the company does next quarter. The common thread is that the data was present but unattached. Nobody wrote down, in advance, which decision the data was supposed to inform or what result would change the plan. Without that link, dashboards become scenery. They make a meeting feel rigorous without making the outcome any more rigorous. Being data-driven is not a property of your tooling. It is a property of how decisions get made. The rest of this guide is about closing that gap. What makes a decision data-driven A decision is data-driven when you can answer four questions before you act: The decision. What specific choice are you making? “Should we raise the Pro plan from $25 to $39?” is a decision. “Understand pricing” is not. The owner. Who makes the final call and is accountable for the outcome? Decisions without a single owner default to the status quo or to whoever has the most authority in the room. The evidence. What numbers, segments, or experiments are you using, and where do they come from? Evidence has to be specific enough that someone else could pull the same query and get the same answer. The threshold. What result would change your mind? If no possible number would change the decision, you are not using data, you are decorating a decision you already made. The fourth question is the one that separates real data-driven teams from theatrical ones. Stating a threshold in advance protects you from the most common analytical sin: looking at the data, then deciding what it “shows” based on what you already wanted to do. If you commit to “we ship if activation among new signups improves by at least three points over four weeks” before the launch, the data can actually tell you something. If you decide after the fact, it cannot. The decision loop Dashboards are continuous, but decisions are discrete. The useful unit of work is a single decision run through a loop. This is the core framework: six steps, with the last two being the ones most teams drop. 1. Frame the question. Write the decision as a single sentence with a clear yes or no, or a small set of options. Vague questions produce vague analysis. Narrow the scope until the question is answerable. 2. Set the threshold first. Before looking at the data, decide what result would push you toward each option. Write it down. This is uncomfortable because it removes your ability to rationalize later, which is exactly the point. 3. Gather the evidence. Pull the specific numbers tied to the decision. Resist the urge to assemble a general dashboard. You want the two or three figures that actually move the choice, segmented the way the decision requires. 4. Decide and write down the reasoning. Make the call. In two or three sentences, record what the evidence showed, how it compared to the threshold, and what you decided. This takes five minutes and saves hours of re-litigation later. 5. Record the decision. Put it somewhere durable: a decision log, a doc, a channel. Include the date, the owner, the evidence, the threshold, and the call. A team that keeps a decision log can answer “why did we do that?” six months later without a forensic investigation. 6. Review the outcome. Set a date to come back and check whether the evidence was right and whether the decision worked. Almost nobody does this, which is why teams repeat the same mistakes. The review is where data-driven decision making compounds. Each closed loop makes the next decision sharper. Steps one through four feel like the work. Steps five and six are what make the work pay off over time. Is your metric decision-grade? Not every number is fit to bet on. Before a metric drives a decision, run it through this rubric. A decision-grade metric should pass all five. Test Question Failure looks like Defined once Is there a single agreed definition for this metric? Three teams report “active users” three different ways Owned Does someone own the definition and its accuracy? Nobody can explain why the number moved Fresh enough Is the data recent enough for this specific decision? Deciding on last quarter’s data because the pipeline is two weeks behind Attributable Can you trace the number back to source rows? A KPI that cannot be drilled into or reproduced Tied to the action Does this metric actually move with the decision? Optimizing a number that has no causal link to the outcome A metric that fails “defined once” creates arguments instead of decisions. One that fails “fresh enough” leads you to act on stale reality. One that fails “tied to the action” is the classic vanity metric: pageviews when the decision is about revenue, signups when the decision is about retention. A practical way to enforce this: when a metric becomes important enough to drive decisions, promote its definition out of individual queries and into a shared layer where everyone references the same logic. This is what a semantic layer is for, and it is also why where you define business metrics matters more than which chart you put them on. The decision brief For decisions that matter, a one-page brief forces the discipline above into a repeatable artifact. It is deliberately short. If it takes more than fifteen minutes to fill in, the decision is either not ready or not actually data-driven yet. Decision: The specific choice, as a single sentence. Owner: The one person accountable for the call. Options: The realistic options, usually two or three. Evidence: The two or three metrics or queries that inform the choice, with links to where they live. Threshold: What result would push toward each option, written before looking. Decision and reasoning: The call and why, in a few sentences. Review date: When you will check whether it worked. Most decisions do not need a brief. Reserve it for choices that are expensive, hard to reverse, or politically contested, the ones where post-hoc rationalization is most tempting. For everyday calls, the four questions from earlier are enough. Common failure modes Even teams with good data and good intentions slide back into instinct. The patterns are consistent. The HiPPO override. The highest paid person’s opinion wins regardless of the data. The fix is not to remove judgment but to name the owner and the threshold in advance, so an override is at least explicit rather than silent. Vanity metrics. The team optimizes numbers that are easy to grow and pleasant to report but disconnected from the actual goal. The decision-grade rubric’s “tied to the action” test exists to catch this. Analysis paralysis. The team keeps pulling more data instead of deciding. This usually means the threshold was never set. If you know in advance what would change your mind, you know when you have enough evidence. Post-hoc rationalization. The decision is made, then the data is selected to justify it. Setting the threshold before looking is the only reliable defense. Metrics without owners. A number moves and a fire drill ensues because nobody knows whether it is real, a pipeline bug, or a definition change. Ownership turns a panic into a five-minute check. The unread dashboard. A dashboard gets built, admired once, and never opened again. This is usually a symptom of the deeper problem: the dashboard was never tied to a recurring decision. For more on this specific failure, see our guide on building dashboards that drive decisions . A maturity model for data-driven decision making Teams tend to move up a ladder. Knowing where you are helps you pick the next improvement instead of buying a tool you are not ready to use. Level 1: Reactive. Decisions are made on instinct and authority. Data is pulled occasionally to justify choices already made. Reports are manual and inconsistent. Level 2: Instrumented. The team has dashboards and tracks KPIs, but the metrics are not consistently tied to decisions. Numbers are visible; their link to action is loose. Most companies that call themselves data-driven are here. Level 3: Decision-grade. Important metrics are defined once and owned. Significant decisions name an owner, evidence, and a threshold in advance. The team trusts the numbers enough to act on them without re-deriving them each time. Level 4: Learning. Decisions are recorded and reviewed. The team systematically checks whether past calls worked and feeds those lessons back into how it decides. This is where the practice compounds, and it is rare. The jump from Level 2 to Level 3 is the hard one, and it is mostly cultural. It requires agreeing on definitions, assigning ownership, and committing to thresholds before the fact. No tool does this for you, though the right tooling removes friction. When not to wait for data A framework for data-driven decisions should also say when to skip it. Treating every choice as a data project is its own failure mode. Cheap, reversible decisions. If a decision is easy to undo and low cost, deciding fast and learning from the result beats a careful analysis. Save the rigor for one-way doors. The cost of waiting exceeds the cost of being wrong. Sometimes a fast, imperfect decision beats a slow, well-supported one because the delay itself is expensive. The data does not exist yet. For genuinely new bets, there is no relevant history. Run a small experiment to generate the data rather than over-analyzing data that does not apply. The decision is about values or strategy. Some choices are about what kind of company you want to be. Data can inform them, but it cannot make them. Good judgment includes knowing which decisions deserve the full loop and which deserve a thirty-second call. How tooling fits Tooling cannot make a team data-driven, but the wrong tooling makes it harder. The friction that pushes teams back toward instinct is usually some combination of: metrics that take too long to pull, definitions that disagree across teams, dashboards nobody can drill into, and a gap between where data lives and where decisions get discussed. The practical requirements are modest. You want metrics defined once and reused, numbers fresh enough for the decision at hand, the ability to drill from a KPI down to the underlying rows, and a short path from a chart to the conversation where the call gets made. Whether that comes from a warehouse plus a semantic layer plus a BI tool, or from a lighter setup that queries your database directly, depends on your stack and team. Basedash is one option in this space, built for teams that want to query a database in plain English, build dashboards quickly, and keep metric definitions consistent without standing up a heavy enterprise BI stack. It fits the smaller, faster end of the spectrum. Heavier platforms like Looker or Tableau fit teams that need a deep modeling layer and have the people to maintain it. The point is not the tool. The point is whether your setup makes it easy to attach a trustworthy number to a specific decision, or whether it adds enough friction that people give up and guess. FAQ What is the difference between data-driven and data-informed? “Data-informed” usually means data is one input among several, including judgment and context. “Data-driven” implies the data carries more weight in the final call. In practice the useful distinction is not the label but whether you set a threshold in advance. If you did, the data is genuinely driving the decision. If you did not, you are data-informed at best and decorating at worst. How do I start if my team makes decisions on instinct today? Pick one recurring, meaningful decision and run it through the loop: frame it, set a threshold, pull the evidence, decide, write it down, and schedule a review. One closed loop teaches more than a new dashboard. Expand from there. Do we need a data warehouse to be data-driven? No. Plenty of small teams make excellent data-driven decisions by querying their production database directly. A warehouse helps when data volume, multiple sources, or query load make direct access painful. Add it when you feel that pain, not before. See our guide on when to add a data warehouse . What is a decision log and is it worth the overhead? A decision log is a durable record of significant decisions, including the date, owner, evidence, threshold, and reasoning. The overhead is a few minutes per decision. It pays off the first time someone asks “why did we do that?” and you can answer in seconds, and again every time it stops the team from repeating a past mistake. How many metrics should drive a single decision? Usually two or three. A decision driven by a dozen metrics is usually a decision without a clear threshold. Identify the figures that actually move the choice and ignore the rest for that specific decision. Can AI make our decisions data-driven for us? AI can lower the friction: generating queries, surfacing anomalies, and drafting summaries. It cannot decide what threshold matters, who owns a decision, or whether a metric is tied to the real goal. Those are judgment calls. AI makes the evidence step faster; it does not replace the framing and the threshold.

title: AECOM appoints David Rottblatt to lead strategic growth across private-sector aviation markets
summary: DALLAS (June 12, 2026) — AECOM, the trusted global infrastructure leader, today announced its appointment of David Rottblatt as Senior Vice President, Director of Strategic Private sector client growth in the Aviation Market Sector. body_text: DALLAS (June 12, 2026) — AECOM, the trusted global infrastructure leader, today announced its appointment of David Rottblatt as Senior Vice President, Director of Strategic Private sector client growth in the Aviation Market Sector. Based out of California, Mr. Rottblatt will be responsible for expanding AECOM’s presence across private sector aviation clients and emerging aviation markets, while strengthening alignment with core commercial airport clients. “We are pleased to welcome David to AECOM,” said Dwight Pullen, Senior Vice President, Global Aviation and Surface Transport Leader. “His deep industry experience, strategic perspective, and proven track record of driving growth across the aviation sector make him an outstanding addition to our team. As the aviation industry continues to evolve, David’s leadership will help us strengthen client relationships, expand into new markets, and deliver even greater value for our clients worldwide.” AECOM continues to grow its aviation business by deepening relationships across the broader aviation ecosystem, including developer-led airport infrastructure partners, private operators, OEMs, logistics providers, and emerging aviation companies. In his new role, Mr. Rottblatt will help strengthen these strategic connections while aligning AECOM’s industry-leading airport delivery, program management, and advisory capabilities with evolving market opportunities. “I am delighted to be joining AECOM at such a pivotal time for the aviation industry,” said Mr. Rottblatt. “As a connector between private-sector and commercial aviation clients, my goal is to demonstrate a commitment to delivering demonstrated value while highlighting our unique capabilities across the aviation system. I look forward to strengthening relationships, driving growth, and capturing opportunities for collaboration across business lines to better serve our clients and partners.” Joining AECOM from Supernal, where he served as the Chief Operating Officer, Mr. Rottblatt brings more than two decades of leadership experience and 15 years in the global aviation industry. Throughout his career he has successfully led high-preforming international teams, developed and scaled strategic go-to-market frameworks, and overseen complex aviation frameworks valued at billions of dollars. His deep expertise in operational excellence, business growth, and industry innovation positions him to further strengthen AECOM’s leadership in the aviation sector. Mr. Rottblatt’s role is effective immediately. About AECOM AECOM is the global infrastructure leader, committed to delivering a better world. As a trusted professional services firm powered by deep technical abilities, we solve our clients’ complex challenges in water, environment, energy, transportation and buildings. Our teams partner with public- and private-sector clients to create innovative, sustainable and resilient solutions throughout the project lifecycle – from advisory, planning, design and engineering to program and construction management. AECOM is a Fortune 500 firm that had revenue of $16.1 billion in fiscal year 2025. Learn more at aecom.com.

Multigres v0.1 Alpha: an operating system for Postgres
summary: Today we're releasing Multigres v0.1 alpha to the open source community, bringing Vitess-grade horizontal scaling, high availability, and operational simplicity to Postgres.
body_text: Today we're releasing Multigres v0.1 alpha to the open source community, the first public milestone of our mission to bring Vitess-grade horizontal scaling, high availability, and operational simplicity to Postgres. It's early, it's alpha, and we're excited to get it into your hands. This is an open-source-only release. Multigres for Supabase is coming soon. What is Multigres? # Multigres is a scalable operating system for Postgres: it holistically manages your Postgres instances and gives you sharding, connection pooling, automatic failover, and backup orchestration. Postgres at scale is operationally complex: You need to manage read replicas, failovers, connection limits, backups, and more. Multigres handles these chores as a single cohesive system. And when the time comes to scale, Multigres will help you shard your database and scale it horizontally. The v0.1 alpha introduces advanced connection pooling, automatic failovers, and a Kubernetes operator for deployment. The Multigres Operator # The Kubernetes Multigres Operator allows you to deploy and manage Multigres clusters on Kubernetes. To get started , you need a Kubernetes cluster along with a location for backups configured. The backups can be a shared file system or a cloud storage bucket like AWS S3. It is also possible to run Multigres on a local Kind cluster. All the necessary images for running Multigres are publicly available. High Availability # Multigres treats HA as a consensus problem, and is capable of resolving split-brain scenarios without losing commits that have succeeded. The protocol implemented by Multigres is based on generalized consensus, a model that gives you flexibilities that do not exist in traditional consensus-based systems: Built on top of Postgres replication : The protocol uses unmodified Postgres replication, and yet satisfies all the strict consistency requirements of a consensus-based system. User-defined durability policies : You can define arbitrarily complex durability policies. This flexibility allows you to specify the failures you are willing to tolerate without being constrained by restrictive rules like a majority quorum. For example, if you'd like your data to survive the failure of a single AZ, you can set your durability policy to be cross-zone, but still have standbys deployed in more than three zones. Add or remove replicas without affecting performance : You can safely scale replicas up and down while the cluster is running. Multigres will continue to honor the durability policy you've configured without affecting performance, while also maintaining correctness. For more information on HA, you may read the following posts: High availability from first principles Handling edge cases using consensus Connection Pooling # Multigres ships its own connection pooling solution using a two-service architecture. It consists of a multigateway that accepts client connections and routes queries, and a multipooler that manages backend connections. This architecture provides some distinct advantages over a single-process pooler. Traffic routing : The integration with the HA system allows multigateway to transparently route connections to the current primary. During a failover, multigateway can hold requests until a new primary is promoted, thereby minimizing errors. Additionally, you can balance read load across multiple replicas. In the future, multigateway will handle routing of traffic to different shards. Context-aware pooling : Multigres does not require you to choose a pooling mode like transaction, session, etc. This is because it has a built-in parser and understands the effects of each request. This allows it to track connection state and reuse them wherever applicable. If a request requires a stateful connection, like a transaction, the connection gets pinned to that client until the stateful requirement is satisfied. Per-user pools : Multigres maintains a separate connection pool per user with no shared pool and no SET ROLE impersonation. A fair-share algorithm splits a fixed connection budget across users, and pool routing is kept fast. Prepared statement consolidation : Multigres deduplicates prepared statements across gateways. Postgres parses, plans, and caches a given statement once, no matter how many gateways are forwarding it. For more information on connection pooling, you may read Two jobs, two processes: why Multigres has its own connection pooler . Backups # Multigres uses pgBackRest for backups. Backups are taken from replicas to avoid overloading the primary. Three backup types : full backups copy the entire data directory at a checkpoint; incremental backups copy only files changed since the previous backup; differential backups copy changes since the last full backup. A typical schedule runs full backups periodically with more frequent incrementals or differentials in between. On-demand and scheduled : the CLI lets you list backups, trigger a manual backup, and initiate a restore. We'll soon add support for scheduled backups through the cluster spec. Bootstrap : During bootstrap, Multigres automatically identifies a primary, performs a backup, and uses it to initialize the other replicas. This workflow brings up a ready-to-run cluster without any manual intervention. To learn more about how a cluster bootstraps, you may read How a Multigres Cluster Bootstraps . What alpha means # v0.1 is stable enough to experiment with and give feedback on. It is not yet ready for production workloads. Specific caveats: We have known issues that still need to be addressed. Sharding (the eventual flagship feature) is not in this release. v0.1 is a single-shard cluster with HA and pooling. Future releases are not guaranteed to be backward compatible. The CR API is not yet stable. Fields may change before v1.0. Performance benchmarks are in progress. We'll publish numbers in a follow-up post. Try Multigres # Deploy your first cluster : a minimal CR that stands up a 3-node HA cluster. Join the community : file issues and request features at github.com/multigres/multigres . Post your thoughts in github.com/multigres/multigres/discussions to discuss features and get help.

title: Bel-Air Apartments Reaches Completion: Finbar's 80th Development
summary: Finbar is proud to announce the completion of our Belmont development, Bel-Air Apartments, thanks to our builder Hanssen Construction, Chang Architects and the many consultants and contractors who have contributed to the construction of this project.
body_text: Finbar is proud to announce the completion of our Belmont development, Bel-Air Apartments, thanks to our builder Hanssen Construction , Chang Architects and the many consultants and contractors who have contributed to the construction of this project. Marking Finbar's 80th completed development, Bel-Air Apartments represents another significant milestone in our commitment to delivering quality apartment living in well-connected locations across Western Australia. Commenting on the project's completion, Finbar CEO Ronald Chan said: "The completion of Bel-Air is a clear example of our objective to deliver mid-level apartment stock that responds to genuine market demand. By focusing on affordability, quality and well-connected locations, we are providing new homes that are accessible to more people without compromising on design, amenity or liveability." The $114 million development comprises 194 one- and two-bedroom apartments, a ground-floor commercial precinct, and an extensive range of resort-style resident facilities designed to support a vibrant and connected lifestyle. Located in the heart of Belmont, Bel-Air Apartments offers residents convenient access to major transport links, employment hubs, retail amenities and recreational destinations, which made it an attractive option for owner-occupiers and investors alike. To celebrate the completion of the development, Finbar hosted the Grand Opening of Bel-Air Apartments on Saturday, welcoming project partners, buyers and special guests. The occasion was marked with a ribbon cutting by Finbar CEO Ronald Chan, Finbar Chairman John Chan, Minister for Housing and Works the Hon John Carey MLA, Hanssen Construction's Gerry Hanssen and Darren Linton, and Chang Architects Director Sin Chang. The completion of Bel-Air highlights Finbar's continued focus on delivering thoughtfully designed developments that meet the evolving needs of Western Australians. We extend our sincere thanks to our valued purchasers, and the dedicated teams from Hanssen Construction and Chang Architects for their contribution to the successful delivery of Bel-Air Apartments. As residents begin moving into their new homes, we look forward to seeing the Bel-Air community flourish and become an integral part of Belmont's growing urban landscape.

title: Investors Tax Guide 2025
summary: Your 2025 tax playbook for investors. Navigate K-1 complexities, capital gains strategies, the TCJA sunset, and new crypto reporting rules before the deadlines.
body_text: Wash Sale Rule: Applicable to Securities Not Yet Crypto The IRS’s wash sale rule under IRC §1091 prohibits deducting a loss if the same or substantially identical security is repurchased within 30 days before or after the sale. This rule currently applies only to securities, not to digital assets such as cryptocurrencies or NFTs. That means investors can, for now: Sell a crypto asset at a loss Realize the tax deduction Immediately repurchase the same token However, proposed regulations have repeatedly targeted this exemption, and there is bipartisan support to close this gap. Best practice: While this loophole remains available in 2025, document all transactions and prepare for the possibility that Congress may extend the wash sale rule to digital assets beginning in 2026. Crypto & Digital Assets: Major Reporting Shift Incoming Draft Form 1099-DA Rules: Reporting Begins for 2025 Transactions Under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, crypto brokers will be required to report digital asset transactions to the IRS. The IRS has released draft Form 1099-DA, and while final regulations are pending, the compliance timeline is clear: Transactions occurring in 2025 will trigger Form 1099-DA filings in 2026 Cost basis reporting will become mandatory in 2027 These rules will apply to: Centralized crypto exchanges Custodial wallet providers Possibly some NFT and DeFi platforms, depending on how the final rules define "broker" Investor action items: Reconcile past transactions (2022–2024) to avoid mismatches once automated IRS data matching begins Implement basis tracking tools—the IRS will begin matching your 8949 filings to broker-issued 1099-DAs Enforcement note: These forms will enable the IRS to systematize enforcement around crypto tax compliance, much like it already does for traditional brokerage accounts. Manual reporting gaps that went unnoticed in previous years will now be easily flagged. International & Alternative Assets Investors holding foreign funds, offshore corporations, collectibles, or niche assets like art, wine, or digital tokens must navigate a thicket of specialized tax rules, many of which carry severe penalties for noncompliance and are tightening in 2025. Passive Foreign Investment Companies (PFICs) Investors in foreign mutual funds, ETFs, offshore hedge funds, or certain crypto-adjacent structures may unknowingly hold PFICs (Passive Foreign Investment Companies), one of the most punitive areas of the tax code. A PFIC is generally any foreign corporation that meets either: The income test: ≥75% of gross income is passive, or The asset test: ≥50% of assets produce passive income Tax impact if not properly elected: Gains are treated as ordinary income, not capital gains Subject to interest charges on tax deferral going back to the original investment year No ability to harvest losses QEF and Mark-to-Market Elections To avoid PFIC default treatment, investors must proactively file one of two elections: Qualified Electing Fund (QEF): Requires annual reporting of your share of ordinary income and capital gains, regardless of distributions Only viable if the foreign fund cooperates and provides PFIC statements (rare in practice) Mark-to-Market (MTM): Only available for marketable securities You report annual unrealized gains as ordinary income Can reduce back-year penalties but accelerates taxable income If you invest in offshore funds through a U.S. feeder, confirm whether the master fund is a PFIC and whether the U.S. vehicle blocks PFIC exposure. Many investors discover PFIC status too late, after IRS Form 8621 is already required. Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) The IRS finalized new foreign tax credit regulations that impact how U.S. investors claim credits for foreign taxes paid, particularly relevant for equity investors, dual-residents, and those earning royalties or dividends abroad. Key change: The “net gain” requirement now demands that foreign tax regimes be reasonably similar to U.S. rules for credits to be allowed. Impact: If a foreign jurisdiction taxes gross revenue rather than net income, the U.S. may deny the foreign tax credit. Many investors with foreign investment platforms or private equity funds may find prior FTC claims disallowed. Rules also scrutinize withholding taxes on dividends or interest if they aren’t imposed on a net-income basis. Planning move: Review all FTC claims for 2023–2025. Reassess how your tax software or preparer classifies each jurisdiction and transaction type under the new rules. Improper FTC claims can result in audit adjustments and interest. Pillar Two & Global Minimum Tax The OECD’s Pillar Two global minimum tax framework imposes a 15% effective minimum tax on large multinationals. But it’s starting to ripple through investment structures, especially those involving foreign-controlled corporations, holding companies, or cross-border SPVs. Key concerns for investors: Top-up taxes may be triggered in countries that have adopted Pillar Two, affecting the after-tax yield of certain international investments. Private funds with foreign portfolio companies may see lower post-tax exit proceeds, even if U.S. tax impact is deferred. Reporting burdens may increase as fund managers push compliance obligations onto investors indirectly (via updated K-1s or side letters). Investor takeaway: Review your exposure to non-U.S. corporate holdings or any structure involving foreign tax jurisdictions adopting Pillar Two. While individuals are not directly taxed under Pillar Two, they can bear the economic cost through reduced returns and greater fund compliance friction. Collectibles and Alternative Assets: The 28% Problem Alternative assets such as art, antiques, coins, wine, and even physical NFTs are subject to collectibles taxation rules. Gains from the sale of these assets—if held more than a year—do not qualify for the standard 20% long-term capital gains rate. Instead, they are taxed at a maximum rate of 28% , plus: 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) if applicable State-level capital gains or income tax, depending on jurisdiction Asset categories taxed as collectibles under IRC §408(m): Artwork Antiques Gems and metals (excluding certain bullion) Stamps and coins (with exceptions) Alcoholic beverages Physical NFTs and certain tokenized real-world assets (gray area but increasingly scrutinized) Consider pairing collectible gains with capital loss harvesting or using a charitable contribution strategy (e.g., donating appreciated art to a 501(c)(3)) to mitigate the high tax cost. Also, document holding periods and appraisals carefully, especially if preparing for a sale or estate inclusion. Real Estate & Passive-Loss Strategies For investors in rental real estate, 2025 presents both challenges and planning windows, particularly around passive loss rules, accelerated depreciation, and the narrowing window on bonus depreciation. Real Estate Professional (REP) Status Most rental activities are considered passive by default under §469, meaning losses can only offset passive income. However, qualifying as a Real Estate Professional (REP) allows active treatment of rental activities, making losses fully deductible against ordinary income. To qualify for REP status: You must spend over 750 hours annually in real estate trades or businesses in which you materially participate. More than 50% of your total working time must be devoted to real estate activities (includes development, brokerage, leasing, operations, etc.). Time spent as an employee doesn’t count unless you own ≥5% of the employer. Planning tip: Grouping elections (under Reg. §1.469-9(g)) can consolidate multiple rental activities for material participation purposes, helping borderline REP filers qualify. Bonus Depreciation: 40% in 2025 Then Gone The sun is setting on one of real estate’s most powerful tax tools. Bonus depreciation, which allows immediate expensing of qualifying property, continues its phaseout: 2025: 40% first-year bonus depreciation (was 60% in 2024). 2026: Drops to 20%. 2027: Fully phased out unless extended by Congress. This is especially relevant when paired with cost segregation studies, which break out shorter-life components (e.g., carpeting, lighting, landscaping) from a property’s structure. These short-life assets often qualify for bonus depreciation, allowing significant upfront deductions. 1031 Exchanges: Don’t Miss the Clock §1031 like-kind exchanges remain a staple for deferring capital gains on real estate. However, the strict timing rules often trip up taxpayers: 45-Day Rule : Identify replacement properties within 45 days of sale. 180-Day Rule : Close on the replacement within 180 days of the sale. These are calendar days, not business days, and no extensions are granted, even for weekends or holidays. Also: Only investment or business-use real estate qualifies (no flips or primary residences). Exchanges must be property-for-property; cryptocurrency, partnership interests, or personal property do not qualify. Retirement & Tax-Deferred Accounts Major policy changes from SECURE 2.0 and sunset-era tax strategy windows are reshaping how high earners and pre-retirees should think about retirement savings. SECURE 2.0 Several provisions from the SECURE 2.0 Act come into effect in 2025, with important implications for contribution strategies and catch-up planning: Mandatory Roth Catch-Up for High Earners : If your wages exceed $145,000 (indexed), all catch-up contributions to employer-sponsored plans (like 401(k)s) must be made on a Roth basis starting in 2025. This could increase current-year tax liabilities but lead to more tax-free income in retirement. Increased Catch-Up Limits (Age 60–63) : In 2025, workers aged 60 to 63 will benefit from enhanced catch-up contributions, up to the greater of $10,000 or 150% of the standard catch-up amount (indexed). Planning around this window can unlock last-minute deferrals before retirement. Student Loan Matching : Employers can start making matching contributions to retirement plans based on qualified student loan payments. This encourages retirement savings even for those focused on debt repayment. Emergency Savings Linked to Roth Accounts : Employees can contribute up to $2,500 into a designated Roth emergency account within employer plans, offering penalty-free access while staying under the retirement umbrella. Roth Conversions 2025 presents a limited window of opportunity for Roth conversions before the TCJA tax bracket sunsets in 2026, when marginal rates are set to rise across income tiers. Strategic considerations include: Harvesting Low Brackets : Converting traditional IRA or pre-tax 401(k) balances into Roth accounts at current lower rates can lock in tax-free growth. This is especially appealing for taxpayers currently in the 22%–24% brackets who expect to be in higher brackets post-2025. State Tax Timing : For taxpayers in states with variable tax regimes, coordinating Roth conversions in years with residency changes or anticipated lower income can amplify net savings. Medicare & NIIT Planning : Be mindful of income thresholds that trigger IRMAA surcharges or the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT). Partial conversions may optimize total tax exposure rather than maximizing the conversion amount. Estate & Gift Planning—Beat the 2026 Cliff Time is running out on the historically high estate and gift tax exemption. Under current law, the lifetime exemption, estimated at $13.99 million per person in 2025—is scheduled to sunset after December 31, 2025, reverting to pre-TCJA levels (roughly $6–7 million per person). For high-net-worth individuals, that means millions in potential tax savings could vanish if action isn’t taken before the cliff. Key Strategies to Consider Before the Sunset 1. Upfront Gifting vs. Portability Upfront gifting lets you lock in today’s high exemption before it disappears. Once used, the IRS won’t “claw back” gifts made under the elevated exemption, per final regulations (Treasury Decision 9884). Gifting removes appreciation from your estate, critical in high-growth asset cases. Portability, where a surviving spouse uses the deceased’s unused exemption, is helpful but: Doesn’t remove asset growth. Requires a timely-filed estate tax return even for non-taxable estates. Only applies to the federal exemption, not available in most states with estate taxes. 2. SLATs (Spousal Lifetime Access Trusts) SLATs allow you to gift assets outside your estate while retaining indirect access through your spouse. Pros: Leverages current exemption. Maintains lifestyle flexibility. Considerations: Can’t name both spouses as beneficiaries of each other’s SLATs, watch for reciprocal trust doctrine risk. Divorce or premature death of the beneficiary spouse could cut off access. 3. GRATs (Grantor Retained Annuity Trusts) GRATs are ideal for low-interest-rate environments or volatile assets. You retain an annuity stream, and excess appreciation passes to heirs gift-tax free. Benefit: No use of exemption if structured as a zeroed-out GRAT. Planning tip: Use rolling short-term GRATs to mitigate mortality risk. 4. Strategic Use of Annual Exclusion Gifts For 2025, the annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient ($368,000 per couple). Consider using 529 plan frontloading, Irrevocable Life Insurance Trusts (ILITs), or Crummey trusts to maximize exclusions while keeping control. Planning Windows Are Narrowing Even if Congress acts to extend or modify the exemption post-2025, there’s no guarantee and retroactive changes are politically unlikely but not impossible. The most prudent strategy is to: Use the exemption while it’s available. Pair gifts with valuation discounts (e.g., for minority or lack-of-marketability interests). Work closely with estate planners to navigate state estate taxes, which often have far lower thresholds. Risk Management & Audit Defense The IRS is significantly ramping up enforcement activity targeting high-income individuals and complex tax structures. With $80 billion in additional funding allocated under the Inflation Reduction Act, the agency is deploying advanced analytics, AI models, and a wave of new auditors to focus on previously under-scrutinized taxpayers and transactions. IRS Targets To Watch In 2025 And Beyond: High-Income Non-Filers : The IRS has explicitly prioritized enforcement against individuals with income over $400,000 who have failed to file returns. In 2024, over 125,000 such cases were flagged, and more automated notices and enforcement actions are expected in 2025. Crypto Asset Tracing And Reporting : With final regulations for Form 1099-DA expected later in 2025, the IRS is sharpening its ability to match crypto transfers across wallets, exchanges, and blockchains. Transfers exceeding $10,000—especially between self-custodied wallets and offshore platforms—are under heavy scrutiny. Taxpayers should prepare for heightened documentation and potential amendments to prior-year filings. Micro-Captive Insurance Schemes : These arrangements, often marketed to closely held businesses, remain on the IRS “Dirty Dozen” list. IRS Notice 2016-66 and subsequent litigation have narrowed the safe harbor for micro-captives. If your business relies on a §831(b) captive, review structure, premiums, and economic substance immediately. Partnership and pass-through audit surge : Under the BBA centralized audit regime, the IRS is increasing exams of complex partnerships and multi-tiered SMLLC structures. The 2025 enforcement wave will emphasize: Inconsistent Schedule K-1 reporting Basis overstatements and capital account misstatements Improper allocations of losses and credits Misapplied PTET benefits across jurisdictions Defensive playbook for high-risk taxpayers: Run mock IRS audits internally or with advisors to assess vulnerabilities. Document positions clearly—keep memos, substantiation, and contemporaneous records. Use protective elections like BBA push-out elections to shift liability to reviewed-year partners. Consider amending returns proactively if risks are identified. Track IRS campaigns and court cases to anticipate shifting audit priorities. Compliance Calendar & Key Deadlines Staying ahead of critical federal and state filing deadlines is non-negotiable in 2025. From estimated tax payments to FATCA and FinCEN reporting, here’s what tax teams must track to avoid penalties and preserve compliance. Estimated Tax Payments (Federal) Quarterly estimated payments are required for individuals, corporations, and pass-through owners who expect to owe $1,000 or more in tax beyond withholding. The 2025 deadlines are: April 15, 2025: 1st quarter (Jan 1 – Mar 31) June 17, 2025: 2nd quarter (Apr 1 – May 31)* September 15, 2025: 3rd quarter (Jun 1 – Aug 31) January 15, 2026: 4th quarter (Sep 1 – Dec 31) *Note: June 15, 2025, is a Sunday; payment due the next business day. Underpayment penalties can apply if safe harbor thresholds (100–110% of prior year tax or 90% of current year liability) are not met. FATCA – Form 8938 (Specified Foreign Financial Assets) U.S. taxpayers holding specified foreign financial assets must file Form 8938 if the value exceeds: Single filers (U.S.-resident): $50,000 at year-end or $75,000 any time during the year Married filing jointly: $100,000 at year-end or $150,000 any time Attach to your federal income tax return (e.g., Form 1040) and file by: April 15, 2025 (or October 15 with a valid extension) Failure to report can trigger substantial penalties, including a $10,000 minimum fine per violation. FinCEN BOI Reporting – Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) Under the CTA, nearly all corporations, LLCs, and similar entities must file Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) reports in 2025. Entities created before March 26, 2025: Must file by April 25, 2025 Entities created on or after March 26, 2025: Must file within 30 calendar days of receiving confirmation of registration (revised from 90 days under new FinCEN rules effective Jan 1, 2025) Exemptions apply for regulated entities (e.g., banks, large operating companies) but must be carefully reviewed. Penalties for noncompliance can reach $500 per day. State PTET (Pass-Through Entity Tax) Deadlines State-specific PTET elections and estimated payments remain a planning lever and compliance obligation: California: PTET prepayment due June 17, 2025, to preserve the annual election Additional payment due by original return date (March 15, 2026) New York: Election due March 15, 2025 Quarterly payments due March 15, June 17, September 16, and December 15, 2025 Other states (e.g., IL, NJ, CT) maintain varied schedules. Use a centralized compliance calendar to track each state’s deadline. Additional Considerations FBAR – FinCEN Form 114: Required for U.S. persons with foreign financial accounts totaling over $10,000 at any time in 2024. Due: April 15, 2025 Automatic extension: October 15, 2025 (no need to request) Disaster Relief Extensions: IRS often extends deadlines for affected regions. For example, taxpayers impacted by 2025 North Carolina storms may have until September 25, 2025, to file certain forms. FAQs How do I know whether a single K-1 will force me to file state tax returns? Not all K-1s trigger state filing requirements, but many do, especially when the underlying entity operates in multiple states. To find out whether your Schedule K-1 for 2024 requires filing a state return, follow these key steps: 1. Identify the Type of K-1 You Received Partnership (Form 1065): Reports your share of income from a partnership. S Corporation (Form 1120-S): Reports shareholder income and deductions. Estate or Trust (Form 1041): Reports beneficiary allocations from fiduciary income. 2. Look for State-Specific Allocations on the K-1 Check for supplemental schedules or footnotes showing income sourced to specific states. On the federal K-1: Box 20 (Partnerships) and Box 17 (S Corporations) may contain state codes. Estates and trusts often note state-sourced income in Part III. 3. Determine if the Income Creates a State Filing Obligation States generally require a return if you earned income sourced to that state, even as a nonresident. Common triggers include rental income, passthrough business income, and gains from in-state activities. 4. Check State Filing Thresholds Some states have surprisingly low thresholds: California: $1,000 of California-sourced income may trigger a return. New York: Similar $1,000 threshold applies for nonresidents. 5. If There Are Multiple States, You May Need Multiple Returns A single K-1 may include income from several states. You may also be eligible for a credit for taxes paid to other states on your home state return. 6. When in Doubt, Get Help If your K-1 includes income from multiple jurisdictions or comes with complex attachments, consult a tax advisor. Mistakes in multi-state filings can lead to interest, penalties, or double taxation. What exactly is a PTET credit, and how do I claim it? The Pass-Through Entity Tax (PTET) credit is a workaround designed by states to help business owners bypass the federal $10,000 cap on state and local tax (SALT) deductions. It allows pass-through entities (PTEs), like partnerships and S corporations, to pay state taxes at the entity level. The business deducts these taxes on its federal return, and the individual owners receive a state tax credit for their share. Here’s how it works: 1. Who qualifies for PTET? Eligible entities include partnerships and S corporations (as defined under state law). The entity must elect into the PTET program—this election is usually annual and irrevocable for that tax year. The owners must be subject to state personal income tax to claim the credit. The IRS confirmed in Notice 2020-75 that PTET payments are deductible by the entity without being limited by the individual SALT cap. 2. How do I claim the PTET credit? Step 1: Make the PTET Election This must be done through a state-specific form or portal. Deadlines vary—some states require the election by the original due date of the entity’s return (without extension). Step 2: Pay the PTET at the Entity Level Payments may be quarterly or annual, depending on the state. The PTE deducts the PTET on its federal return (Form 1065 or 1120-S). Step 3: Claim the Credit as an Owner Each owner reports their share of the PTET paid and claims a credit on their personal state return. 3. Examples of PTET Programs by State California (AB 150): Annual election required. Credit is claimed on Form 540. New York: Opt-in deadline is March 15. Owners use their NY personal return to claim the credit. Connecticut: PTET is mandatory, and the credit is automatically applied to owners. Each state has different mechanics, so consult specific guidance to stay compliant. 4. Required Forms Federal return : Use Form 1065 (partnerships) or Form 1120-S (S corps) to report the PTET deduction. State return : Varies by jurisdiction (e.g., CA Form 540, NY IT-204-LL). 5. Important Considerations Estimated payments may be required during the year. Double taxation risks exist if you’re taxed in multiple states—coordinate credits carefully. Irrevocability: Once made, the PTET election can’t be undone for that tax year. I hold a foreign fund—should I make a QEF election or rely on the PFIC high-tax exception? It depends on your specific tax goals, access to information from the fund, and the foreign jurisdiction’s tax rate. Both options, Qualified Electing Fund (QEF) election and the PFIC high-tax exception, offer ways to reduce the punitive tax treatment under the Passive Foreign Investment Company (PFIC) rules. But each has its own tradeoffs in terms of tax timing, reporting burden, and eligibility. Here’s a breakdown to help you choose the best option: 1. Understanding PFIC status A foreign corporation is classified as a PFIC if it meets either of the following tests: Income Test: 75% or more of its gross income is passive (e.g., dividends, interest). Asset Test: 50% or more of its assets produce—or are held to produce—passive income. If your fund meets either test, PFIC rules apply unless you qualify for an exception or make an election. 2. What is a QEF election? A QEF election (under Section 1295) lets you avoid deferred taxation and interest penalties by reporting your pro rata share of the fund’s ordinary earnings and capital gains annually—similar to U.S. mutual funds. Pros: Avoids excess distribution penalties under Section 1291. Allows for long-term capital gains treatment. Cons: Requires cooperation from the fund to provide annual PFIC statements. You must file Form 8621 every year with detailed income and gain disclosures. 3. What is the PFIC high-tax exception? The high-tax exception (under Section 1297(b)(2)(B)) lets you exclude certain passive income from PFIC classification if it’s taxed at a high rate abroad—specifically, if the effective foreign tax rate exceeds 90% of the highest U.S. corporate rate (i.e., above 18.9% as of 2025). Pros: Avoids PFIC status entirely for qualifying income. May reduce annual reporting under Section 1298(f). Cons: Requires careful tracking and proof of effective foreign tax rates. Less predictable if foreign taxes or the fund’s income mix changes. 4. Key factors to consider A. Tax timing & flexibility QEF : Pay U.S. tax on earnings as they arise—good for long-term planning. High-tax exception : Defer income unless distributed, but only works if foreign tax rates remain high. B. Reporting requirements QEF : More paperwork (Form 8621) but clear guidance. High-tax exception : Fewer forms, but higher audit risk if foreign tax details are missing or inconsistent. C. Fund cooperation QEF only works if the foreign fund provides an annual PFIC information statement—this is often not available for hedge funds or pooled investments outside U.S. structures. 5. When to choose which? Use QEF if the fund cooperates and you’re in it for the long haul. It’s more transparent, avoids penalty taxes, and ensures clean exit taxation. Use the high-tax exception if the fund is in a jurisdiction like Germany or France with consistently high taxes, and you don’t want to rely on fund cooperation. 6. Forms and references Form 8621 – Required for both QEF elections and high-tax exception reporting. IRC Section 1295 – Details the QEF regime. IRC Section 1297 – Covers PFIC definitions and high-tax rules. What happens to my estate plan if the lifetime exemption falls after 2025? If the lifetime estate and gift tax exemption decreases after 2025 as scheduled, it could significantly affect your estate plan. The exemption—currently set at $13.99 million per individual—is expected to drop to roughly $6–7 million (adjusted for inflation) beginning in 2026, unless Congress acts to extend current levels. This reduction means more of your estate could become subject to federal estate tax, which has a top rate of 40%. However, the IRS has clarified that gifts made before the exemption sunsets will not be retroactively taxed. For example, if you gift $10 million in 2025, that amount remains exempt even if the exemption later drops. To mitigate potential exposure, consider making large gifts before 2026. Strategies like irrevocable trusts, spousal lifetime access trusts (SLATs), and family limited partnerships can help move appreciating assets out of your taxable estate. Married couples can also preserve unused exemption through portability, which must be elected via a timely filed estate tax return. This can effectively double the exemption for joint estates. Given the uncertainty around future tax law, reviewing your estate plan now is critical. Acting in advance allows you to lock in today’s higher exemption and implement tax-efficient structures tailored to your long-term goals.

title: Snap Launches New Tools for SPECS Developers
summary: Whether you’re starting from scratch or bringing work you’ve already built, new Lens Studio tools make it easier to create for SPECS
body_text: Today at AWE, we unveiled SPECS: a new kind of computer designed for real life, built into see-through glasses. SPECS are built from the ground up for augmented reality, so computing can move out of your pocket and into the world around you where life actually happens. That shift creates a huge opportunity for developers. Instead of adapting phone apps to a new screen, developers can build experiences that understand the space around you, respond in the moment, and feel useful, shared, playful, and full of wonder. And we want to make it easier than ever to build them. Lens Studio started as a tool for making Snapchat Lenses. Today, it’s a powerful developer environment for real-world, immersive, and connected AR experiences. Over the past year and a half, we’ve shipped 10 Snap OS updates with more than 40 new features and APIs, and developers have already published hundreds of Lenses for SPECS. Now, we’re introducing new tools and programs to help developers move faster — whether they’re exploring an idea, testing on device, bringing over existing work, or building a business. A new agentic development framework First, we’re rolling out the developer preview of agentic development for building SPECS Lenses in Lens Studio. This brings Lens Studio agents and skills into the AI tools developers already use, including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. It can help with the repetitive but important parts of building: exploring ideas, prototyping, testing, debugging, optimizing, publishing, and improving experiences after they ship. Developers stay in control by reviewing suggestions, steering the creative direction, and making final decisions. A new benchmark for spatial AI We’re also releasing the SPECS Spatial Benchmark to help developers understand how AI models perform on real-world spatial tasks — like reasoning about layouts, coordinates, object relationships, and how digital content should respond to the physical world. Bringing existing work to SPECS For teams with existing projects, we’re introducing new ways to bring that work to SPECS. Our Migration Agent helps port projects from tools like Unity into Lens Studio by translating project structures, visual components, and scene configurations into native Lens Studio structures. And our new Native Development Kit lets developers bring C and C++ code directly into Lenses, so teams can reuse performance-critical work across areas like spatial mapping, physics, audio, networking, and navigation. Partners are already putting these tools to work. Niantic Spatial is bringing their VPS to SPECS through the NDK, powering immersive real-world experiences. And Mapbox ported its Navigation Engine in less than two hours. At launch, Commerce Kit will begin powering in-Lens purchases and subscriptions, so developers can build real businesses. Join the SPECS Developer Program Developers can join the SPECS Developer Program and start building with the new Lens Studio agents and skills today. Developers can also apply to test their best Lens prototypes on SPECS at Snap studios around the world, giving developers a chance to see how their ideas perform on hardware, refine their experiences, and prepare for this next generation of computing. We can’t wait to see what you create!

body_text: Over the past few years, few food topics have generated as much discussion as ultra-processed foods, commonly referred to as UPFs. Consumers are increasingly scrutinizing ingredient lists, questioning processing methods, and looking for foods they perceive as less processed. In response, a growing number of brands are beginning to market products using terms like "Non-UPF" or "Not Ultra-Processed." But what does a Non-UPF claim actually mean? Unlike claims such as USDA Organic or Non-GMO Project Verified, there is currently no universally recognized regulatory definition or certification program for Non-UPF foods. That has created both opportunities and challenges for brands looking to respond to consumer demand while maintaining credibility. Photo Credit: https://www.instagram.com/p/DY-L6FLjzhU/ What Does “Ultra-Processed Food (UPF)” Mean? Most discussions about ultra-processed foods trace back to the NOVA food classification system, a framework developed by researchers to categorize foods according to the nature, extent, and purpose of processing. The NOVA system divides foods into four categories: Unprocessed or minimally processed foods Processed culinary ingredients Processed foods Ultra-processed foods Under the NOVA classification system, ultra-processed foods are generally described as industrially formulated products that contain ingredients or substances not commonly used in home kitchens, often combined with multiple processing techniques. Examples frequently cited include: Soft drinks Confectionery products Packaged snack foods Certain ready-to-eat meals Some highly formulated bakery products IMAGE: https://www.winssolutions.org/nova-food-classification-guide/ However, the ultra-processed food definition continues to be debated. Researchers, regulators, manufacturers, and nutrition experts do not always agree on where specific products should fall within the classification system. This lack of consensus is one reason why Non-UPF claims have become such a complex topic. What Is a Non-UPF Claim? A Non-UPF claim generally suggests that a product does not meet the criteria for being classified as ultra-processed. The challenge is that there is currently no universally accepted definition of a non-ultra processed food label. Some brands rely on NOVA classifications, while others evaluate additional factors related to ingredients, formulation, and processing methods. Retailers may also establish their own requirements when evaluating products marketed as Non-UPF. As a result, two products making similar Non-UPF claims may be using different methodologies to support those claims. This is one reason why the conversation has shifted beyond ingredient lists alone and toward the broader question of how these claims can be substantiated. "72% of shoppers say they are seeking to avoid ultraprocessed foods" - Non-UPF Verified Program Are Non-UPF Claims Regulated? Not at this time. Unlike claims such as USDA Organic, there is currently no federal regulation in the United States that defines Non-UPF as a formal food labeling claim. There is also no government-managed certification program that determines whether a product qualifies as Non-UPF. That does not mean companies can make misleading claims. Food labeling rules still require claims to be truthful and not deceptive. At the same time, a third-party verification program has emerged to provide greater consistency around Non-UPF claims. The Non-UPF Verified™ program establishes criteria that products must meet in order to carry a verified Non-UPF designation, helping bring greater transparency to an evolving category. Can Non-UPF Claims Be Verified? The emergence of the Non-UPF Verified™ Standard has established a framework for evaluating products against defined criteria related to ingredients, formulation, and processing methods associated with ultra-processing. Verification requires clear, measurable requirements. Products seeking verification are evaluated against established criteria, which may include ingredient composition, processing methods, functional additives, formulation complexity, and supporting documentation. As with any verification program, the credibility of the claim depends on the clarity, consistency, and transparency of the standard being applied. Verification is not simply about determining whether a product is "good" or "bad." It is about evaluating whether a product meets a defined standard and whether that determination can be supported through documentation and review. By employing a clear and robust Non-UPF Verified Program claim, supported by a third-party verifier such as Where Food Comes From, brands and retailers can effectively convey this new and significant message to their consumers. What This Means for Brands and Retailers For brands, Non-UPF positioning represents both an opportunity and a responsibility. Consumer interest in food processing, ingredient transparency, and product formulation is clearly growing. Products that align with those preferences may gain attention in an increasingly competitive marketplace. At the same time, the lack of universal agreement around ultra-processing creates challenges. "81% of shoppers want to know more about why food ingredients banned in other countries are still used in the US" - Non-UPF Verified Project Learn More When claims are built on unclear or inconsistent criteria, it can become difficult for retailers, buyers, and consumers to understand what those claims actually mean. This is where transparent methodologies, clearly defined standards, and verification frameworks become increasingly important. Regardless of how the category evolves, claims should be supported by criteria that can be consistently applied, evaluated, and communicated. Looking Ahead The conversation around ultra-processed foods is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. As consumer interest grows, more brands will likely explore Non-UPF positioning and seek ways to communicate how their products are formulated and processed. For brands considering Non-UPF positioning, the focus should not simply be on making the claim. It should be on ensuring the claim can be clearly explained, consistently applied, and supported with evidence.

title: Defense Obsolescence Management: Escaping Legacy Gaps
summary: Discover how smart obsolescence management and product life cycle extension resolve the conflict between multi-decade platforms and short component lifecycles.
body_text: Home Blogs Defense Obsolescence Management: Escaping Legacy Gaps Defense Obsolescence Management: Escaping Legacy Gaps Ryan Lawson | Paul Cahill Engineering Manager | Senior Engineering Customer Development Manager • June 18, 2026 • 5 min read Designing Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Share on Mail (Opens in new window) Mail Key Takeaways The Lifecycle Gap: Deployed military platforms outlast commercial electronic component lifecycles by decades, causing severe sustainment challenges. Preserving Data: Forensic engineering analysis allows defense primes to extract lost design data and establish an authoritative digital thread. Targeted Modernization: Implementing Design for Manufacturability (DFM) and engineering gate reviews minimizes validation scope and avoids full-scale recertification costs. The defense industry is reaching a critical tipping point. Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and primes face a systemic, compounding burden: maintaining complex, aging platforms while under immense pressure to accelerate New Product Introduction (NPI) . This operational tension drains capital, monopolizes engineering talent and compromises long-term innovation. At its core, the problem is a direct conflict between the exceptionally long service life of military platforms, which routinely last 25 years or more, and the rapid obsolescence cycles of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) electronic components, which typically span just five to seven years. When engineers are constantly pulled into reactive firefighting to keep a legacy product operational, they cannot focus on next-generation development. The Interconnected Triple Burden: Finance, Knowledge and Certification Sustaining legacy systems places three distinct, compounding pressures on defense organizations: Escalating Life Cycle Costs: Managing component degradation across aging fleets is an immense financial drain. Non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs linked to aircraft obsolescence alone are estimated to cost the global defense sector between $50 billion and $70 billion . Shifting Workforce Dynamics: The industry faces an imminent talent cliff, with up to 29% of the aerospace and defense workforce currently eligible for retirement. As these senior specialists exit, organizations lose decades of undocumented tribal knowledge. Vital design data often vanishes with them, leaving behind incomplete schematics and unrecorded engineering modifications. Rigorous Regulatory Compliance: Modernizing an aerospace or defense asset requires managing rigorous international regulatory frameworks, including the UK Ministry of Defense (MOD), NATO and the US Department of Defense (DoD) standards. Without an authoritative digital thread, even minor component changes can trigger a mandatory, full-scale system recertification, accumulating massive costs and multi-year delays. Shifting from Reactive Repair to Product Life Cycle Extension To break free from this cycle, defense primes should transition from reactive, short-term maintenance to proactive sustainment. When original documentation is missing, altered or obsolete, Plexus delivers comprehensive aftermarket services focused on product life cycle extension . Through systematic engineering analysis, engineers can deconstruct legacy assemblies, map signal dependencies and rebuild missing documentation from physical hardware. This deep technical investigation establishes a reliable baseline of design data, allowing organizations to treat an old asset as a sustainable product capable of controlled, future updates. Rather than executing hasty component swaps that create secondary supply chain issues, this disciplined baseline approach ensures that every modification protects the structural integrity of the wider system architecture. Can We Update Legacy Systems Without Full Recertification? Modernizing legacy systems without triggering a complete platform overhaul requires isolating changes to specific subsystems. The most efficient path to legacy system modernization is not a complete, top-down system redesign. Complete overhauls require exhaustive recertification, which amplifies engineering risk and delays deployment. Instead, a targeted approach limits the scope of verification to the specific subsystem undergoing modification. By applying a disciplined life cycle gate process, moving methodically from System Requirements Review (SRR) through Preliminary Design Review (PDR) and Critical Design Review (CDR), engineering teams can isolate modifications. This ensures that only the modified sub-assemblies face rigorous testing, leaving the broader, pre-certified platform architecture untouched. Case Study: Subsystem Modernization in Action When a core communications processor within a deployed military vehicle intercom system faced critical component obsolescence, production lines were threatened with immediate disruption. A complete system overhaul would require multi-year, platform-level recertification. The Challenge: Bypass a total system redesign while protecting the broader platform architecture from mandatory recertification. The Plexus Solution: Our engineering team designed a custom daughterboard interface module. Utilizing a modern, readily available processor, this self-contained module provided an exact form, fit and functional replication of the obsolete component, confining the testing and verification scope entirely to the interface itself. The Result: The strategic remediation bypassed full-platform recertification, completed development in just nine months, and extended the product’s life by over a decade. Supply Chain Resiliency: Mitigate Risk with Real-Time Analytics True obsolescence management requires combining rigorous engineering with predictive supply chain analytics. Siloed engineering choices often lead to long-term procurement challenges if components are selected without considering future availability. Advanced predictive tools, such as DRIVE analytics and the ALARM™ lifecycle risk assessment tool, allow Plexus’ supply chain teams to monitor component lifecycles in real time. This data enables our teams to anticipate end-of-life notices long before they disrupt production. Integrating DFM principles early in the remediation process ensures that replacement components are selected for both their performance and their long-term supply stability. By evaluating manufacturing tolerances, component lead times and second-source availability during the design phase, primes can mitigate supply chain friction and build resilient, long-term support models. Redirecting Capital for Next-Generation Innovation Every hour an engineer spends reverse-engineering an obsolete circuit board is an hour lost on new product development. Outsourcing the technical burden of sustainment to a trusted operational partner allows defense primes to reallocate their internal talent to high-value, next-generation innovation. At Plexus, engineering services is fundamental to our identity. We partner with defense leaders to transform legacy maintenance from a reactive, unpredictable expense into a disciplined, strategic advantage. Our global expertise across Design & Development , Supply Chain solutions and specialized Sustaining Services ensures your complex legacy products remain mission-ready, allowing your team to focus confidently on designing the future.
